title: Find Your Freedom Number
body:
Financial freedom means different things to different people: no debt, more time with family, travel, or simply making work optional. Whatever yours is, it has a price tag, and knowing it turns a dream into a plan.

The rule of thumb: you are financially free when your investments can pay your yearly spending. At a 4% safe withdrawal rate, that is 25 times your annual expenses.

• Spend $3,000 a month → $36,000 a year → freedom number $900,000
• Spend $2,000 a month → $24,000 a year → freedom number $600,000

Notice the lever: every $100 you cut from monthly spending lowers the target by $30,000, and you save that $100 too. Spending less helps twice.

Write down what freedom means to you in one sentence. Then let the number tell you how far away it is.

title: Budget in 15 Minutes
body:
You can't save money you can't see. A budget is not a punishment; it's a map of where your money already goes.

Do it once, in 15 minutes:

1. Income: add up everything that lands in your account each month after tax: paycheck, side work, interest, dividends.
2. Expenses: open last month's bank and card statements and list every charge: rent, bills, insurance, food, subscriptions, fun.
3. Subtract: income minus expenses is what you can save.

Most people are surprised by step 2. Small charges hide in plain sight: three streaming services, daily coffee, delivery fees.

The goal isn't a perfect spreadsheet. It's one honest number: how much is left at the end of the month. Once you know it, you can decide where it goes, instead of wondering where it went.

title: Pay Yourself First: The 10% → 20% Ladder
body:
If you save whatever is left at the end of the month, there is rarely anything left. Flip it: save first, then live on the rest.

Start with a step you can keep:

• Step 1: save 10% of your take-home pay. On $3,500 a month, that's $350.
• Step 2: once that feels normal, raise it to 15%.
• Step 3: aim for 20% or more. On $3,500, that's $700 a month.

The trick is automation. Set an automatic transfer for the day after payday, so the money moves before you can spend it. You stop relying on willpower, and the habit runs itself.

Raise the rate whenever your income goes up. If you get a raise, save at least half of it, and your lifestyle still improves while your savings grow faster.

Try it in MyPortfolioBuddy: your savings rate is on the FIRE page. Watch how each extra 5% moves your FIRE date closer.

title: Make Your Cash Work: High-Yield Accounts
body:
Money sitting in a traditional savings account can earn close to nothing. A high-yield savings account (HYSA) often pays far more for the same safety.

The difference on $10,000 in a year:

• At 0.01%: about $1
• At 4%: about $400

Same money, same safety (look for deposit insurance), very different result.

A simple setup:

• Checking: enough for about two months of bills.
• High-yield savings: your emergency fund and short-term goals.
• Certificates of deposit (CDs): money you won't need for 3–12 months. A CD locks in today's rate, which helps when rates are expected to fall.

Rates change, so compare a few banks once a year and move your cash if yours falls behind.

Try it in MyPortfolioBuddy: add savings accounts and CDs as incomes with their balance and APY. Their interest shows up in your income and grows in your FIRE projection.

title: Your Safety Net: 3–6 Months of Expenses
body:
Flat tires, burst pipes, vet bills, a lost job: something always happens. An emergency fund means those moments cost you money, not your plans.

How much:

• Multiply your monthly expenses by 3 for the minimum and by 6 for a full fund.
• Example: $2,000 a month → $6,000 to $12,000.
• Lean toward 6 months (or more) if your income is irregular or you support others.

Where: a high-yield savings account. It should be safe and easy to reach within a day or two, and not invested in stocks, which can be down exactly when you need the money.

How fast: saving 20% of your pay, most people build it in about a year. Automate a monthly transfer and treat it like a bill.

If you ever use it, refilling it becomes the next goal before anything else.

title: 8 Expenses to Cut This Month
body:
Cutting costs is the fastest raise you can give yourself, with no interview and no tax on it. Go through these eight:

1. Insurance: compare car and home quotes once a year; 10 minutes can save hundreds.
2. Eating out: cook most meals at home. A $4 home lunch beats a $16 one, five days a week.
3. Subscriptions: list every recurring charge and cancel what you don't use every week.
4. Impulse buys: wait 48 hours before any non-essential purchase, and shop with a list.
5. Utilities: fix leaks, switch off what you don't use, and avoid peak-rate hours.
6. Transport: carpool, take transit, or bike. If your car costs more than about 15% of your pay, consider a reliable used one.
7. Fun: swap pricey outings for parks, museums, game nights, and free events.
8. Housing: the biggest line for most people. A smaller place or a roommate can free up hundreds a month.

Pick three, write down what each saves, and move that amount to savings on the day you cut it.

Try it in MyPortfolioBuddy: give expenses an end date when you cancel them, and see the change in your FIRE date right away.

title: Snowball or Avalanche? Pick Your Debt Plan
body:
High-interest debt works against you every month. Two proven ways to pay it off, both start the same way: list every debt with its balance and interest rate (APR), and pay the minimum on all of them.

Then put every extra dollar on one debt at a time:

• Snowball: smallest balance first. You get quick wins, and each payoff frees up money for the next. Best if motivation is your challenge.
• Avalanche: highest interest rate first. You pay the least interest overall. Best if you want the math to work hardest for you.

Example with $700 a month to spare and three debts (a $2,000 card at 22%, a $3,000 card at 18%, and a $5,000 car loan at 8%): the avalanche attacks the 22% card first, then the 18% card, then the car loan.

While you're paying off debt, keep a small cash cushion so a surprise doesn't land on a credit card again.

Try it in MyPortfolioBuddy: add debt payments as expenses (Loans & finance) with their end dates, and watch your monthly cash free up as each one ends.

title: Credit Scores, Decoded
body:
Your credit score is your financial report card. A higher score means lower interest rates on cars, homes, and loans, which can save tens of thousands over a lifetime.

FICO scores run from 300 to 850: 580–669 is fair, 670–739 good, 740–799 very good, and 800+ exceptional.

Five habits that raise it over time:

1. Pay the full statement balance every month. Then you pay no interest at all. Turn on autopay so you never miss a date.
2. Keep utilization low: use under 30% of your total credit limit, ideally under 10%. With $20,000 in limits, keep balances under $2,000.
3. Keep old cards open: a long history helps. Use each one for a small purchase every few months so it stays active.
4. Space out applications: wait at least 3–6 months between new cards to limit hard inquiries.
5. Check your report once a year for mistakes, and dispute anything that isn't yours.

A credit card used this way costs nothing and builds your score. Carrying a balance does the opposite.

title: Free Money First: The 401(k) Match
body:
If your employer matches 401(k) contributions, that match is an instant 100% return. Nothing else in investing reliably comes close.

How it works: say your employer matches up to 5% of your salary and you earn $80,000. Contribute $4,000 a year and your employer adds $4,000. You just turned $4,000 into $8,000 before any market growth.

Three steps:

1. Ask HR exactly how the match works and whether it vests over time.
2. Contribute at least enough to get the full match. Anything less leaves free money behind.
3. Choose a low-cost broad index fund, such as an S&P 500 or total-market fund.

Watch the fees. An expense ratio of 1% sounds small, but over a career it can cost tens of thousands of dollars. Look for funds well under 0.5%; many index funds charge under 0.1%.

Once you're getting the full match, the next dollar usually goes to a Roth IRA.

Rules and limits vary by plan and change over time; check yours.

title: Roth IRA vs. Taxable Account
body:
After the 401(k) match, two accounts do most of the work.

Roth IRA (a US individual retirement account):

• You put in money you've already paid tax on.
• It grows tax-free, and qualified withdrawals after age 59½ are tax-free too.
• There are yearly contribution limits and income limits, set by the IRS and updated over time.

Taxable brokerage account:

• No contribution limits, and you can withdraw anytime.
• You pay tax on dividends and on gains when you sell.
• Ideal once your Roth IRA is maxed, or for goals before retirement.

Opening either takes about 10 minutes at a large, low-cost brokerage. You'll need your ID and bank details.

The step many people miss: depositing money is not investing. After the deposit, you have to buy something, such as a broad index fund. Set up an automatic monthly deposit and an automatic purchase so it happens without thinking.

Outside the US, look for your country's tax-advantaged account (for example, a TFSA in Canada).

title: Own 500 Companies in One Purchase
body:
Picking winning stocks is hard, even for professionals. An S&P 500 index fund skips the guessing: one purchase gives you a slice of 500 of the largest US companies.

Why beginners start here:

• Built-in diversification: one company's bad news barely moves it.
• Low cost: many charge under 0.1% a year.
• Simple: no research, no timing, no constant decisions.

How to do it:

1. Pick one fund from a major provider; they track the same index.
2. Invest a fixed amount every month, no matter what the market does.
3. Hold for years, not weeks. Markets fall sometimes; steady buying through the dips is how long-term investors win.

Can't afford a whole share? Many brokerages sell fractional shares, so $50 still buys in.

The biggest risk isn't picking the wrong fund. It's not starting, or selling in a panic.

title: Your Paycheck Flowchart
body:
Every paycheck, the same question: where should the next dollar go? Follow this order, and move to the next step only when the current one is done.

1. High-interest debt: pay it down first (snowball or avalanche).
2. Checking cushion: about two months of bills.
3. Emergency fund: 3–6 months of expenses in high-yield savings.
4. 401(k) match: contribute enough to get every matched dollar.
5. Roth IRA: contribute up to the yearly limit and buy low-cost index funds.
6. HSA, if you have a high-deductible health plan: another tax-advantaged account that can double as retirement savings.
7. Taxable brokerage: everything left over, invested the same simple way.

Aim to send 20% of your take-home pay down this list every month. Start at 10% if you need to, and raise it with every raise.

It's not about being perfect. It's about knowing exactly what the next dollar does.

title: Build a Wealth Mindset
body:
Most millionaires didn't inherit their money or win the lottery. They earned ordinary incomes and kept steady habits: they budgeted, avoided expensive debt, and invested every month for years.

Habits beat talent. Three ways to build them:

1. Surround yourself with people who talk about money openly. You tend to become like the people you spend time with, so find a group, online or in person, that is building wealth too.
2. Keep learning a little at a time. One article a week compounds just like money does.
3. Read books that change how you think. Three good places to start are The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel, Atomic Habits by James Clear, and The Simple Path to Wealth by JL Collins.

Most of all, act. Reading about money without changing anything is like watching cooking videos and expecting dinner. Pick one action from any article here and do it this week.
